Towns Like Yellow Springs

Phase 1 of the small-town screen · built November 3, 2026

Towns Like Yellow Springs

Every town and village in the US from 1,500 to 60,000 people, scored on how closely it matches Yellow Springs, Ohio, on six traits: an educated population, a college anchor, arts and civic life, progressive politics, a walkable historic center, and being its own town rather than a suburb. A town that beats Yellow Springs on a trait gets full credit for it. Mountains, schools, climate, airports and prices come in Phase 2.

    How it's scored

    • Minimum likeness hides towns below the cutoff on both the map and the table; set it to All to see every town. Likeness averages the six traits, each scored against Yellow Springs: a town at or above Yellow Springs' level gets full credit, and one at half its level gets half. Trait numbers in the table are percentiles among the nation's 2,000–40,000-person towns (100 is highest).
    • Educated: adults 25 and older with a bachelor's degree or more (Census ACS 2020–24).
    • College: the strongest degree-granting college within about 2 km of the town (federal IPEDS directory). Liberal arts colleges count fully; regional and research universities count about three-quarters; community colleges about a third. Census places that are just a campus (such as "Vassar College") are left out as towns.
    • Arts and civic life: arts and culture nonprofits per resident, the subset with at least $50,000 in revenue, environmental and food or farm nonprofits per resident (IRS exempt-organization file, matched by mailing town and ZIP), plus the share of workers in arts, design and media jobs. Mailing towns include their surrounding countryside, so very small towns can look busier than they are.
    • Progressive: the Democratic share of the two-party vote in the 2020 presidential election, from precincts inside the town (New York Times precinct map). Where a state's precinct data is incomplete, the county's 2024 result is used, nudged 2.5 points toward 2020 levels, and marked in Notes; that is much rougher, because a blue village in a red county looks red.
    • Walkable: the EPA's national walkability index for the town's most walkable neighborhood, the share of homes built before 1940, and the share of commuters who walk or bike.
    • Distinct town: full credit outside any urban area of 50,000 or more, less inside one, and least inside one of 150,000 or more, blended with the share of workers who work in their own town.
    • Median home value is what owners estimate their homes are worth, averaged over 2020–24 (Census ACS), so it runs behind today’s prices, often by 10–20% in places that have risen fast. The Census caps it at $2 million. Phase 2 will add Zillow’s current figures. With the slider set, towns without a value are left out.
    • Airport drive is the road drive time from the town to the nearest airport with nonstop flights to Columbus (John Glenn or Rickenbacker), using the route list Columbus Navigator updated October 19, 2026, and OpenStreetMap routing. Those drive times assume no traffic but run somewhat long on rural highways (Oberlin to Detroit shows 2h36, where it's usually about two hours). “Daily, year-round” counts the 35 airports with daily service all year; “Year-round” adds 7 served only by Allegiant or Breeze, usually a few times a week; “Any” adds 12 seasonal routes. Towns near Columbus simply drive there, so their profile also shows the drive to downtown Columbus; direct driving will become its own option later. Hawaii and a few Alaska towns have no road route and are left out when the slider is set.
    • Notes flags: college-dominated means more than 30% of residents are college students; resort means more than a quarter of homes are seasonal or second homes; suburb means the town sits inside a big city's urban area.
